rationale: A wins because it stays cleaner on what the update actually supports. Its strongest angle, "Skydio says its power-line drones fly with no pilot at all — regulators will want specifics," turns the biggest claim into a defensible reporting question instead of pretending the proof exists. B has sharp instincts, especially "A drone with no pilot is a shot at the inspection business built on pilots," but it starts building a labor-displacement story before the facts have earned that load. And "docks at the substation" is the kind of cute specificity that gets you corrected.
gaps_in_A: "Power-line and substation inspection is dangerous, manual, and expensive work utilities have wanted to automate for years" adds context that may be true, but it is not in the supplied update and needs sourcing.
"the first major public proof point since the consumer exit" overclaims unless you know Skydio has had no other enterprise proof points in the past two years.
"a live, contracted enterprise product" is a little too confident. The update says launch plus contracts, not live deployments.
"the restrictions themselves are already in effect" needs verification; the update only says Chinese drone makers are facing import restrictions.
gaps_in_B: "docks at the substation" invents a location. The update says the drone docks and inspects substations, not that the dock sits at a substation.
"the inspection business built on pilots" is an attractive conflict, but it assumes a services-market displacement story not established by the update.
"who loses the contract when the dock wins it" is a good reporter question, but as framed it presumes contract replacement before any customer or deployment detail is disclosed.
"first hard evidence of whether the two-year-old pivot produced a real enterprise product" overclaims. The facts support a launch and claimed utility contracts, not a full verdict on the pivot.
